planting.note: Sow or transplant into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; this Madeira-native shrub resents summer irrigation once established and rots quickly in heavy or wet ground. It is hardy to about 25 degrees F and thrives in coastal, fog-influenced climates such as much of coastal California.

directions: Plant in lean, gravelly or sandy soil with excellent drainage and full sun; Pride of Madeira forms a rounded, woody-based shrub with rosettes of long, silver-gray, felted leaves that erupt each spring into dozens of dense, curving spikes of small blue-purple (occasionally pink or white) flowers, each spike resembling a giant caterpillar. It is an outstanding bee and butterfly plant, drawing huge numbers of honeybees, bumblebees, and migrating monarchs during its long spring-to-summer bloom. Once established it needs little to no supplemental water and actually declines with rich soil or regular irrigation, making it a favorite for coastal xeriscape and cliffside plantings. Cut back hard after flowering to keep the shrub compact, as older plants become leggy and woody; it is naturalized along the California coast, where it self-sows in disturbed, well-drained sites.

planting.note: Sow directly in lean, sharply drained, alkaline-to-neutral soil in full sun; native to the arid volcanic slopes of Mount Teide on Tenerife, this species demands minimal water and poor soil to avoid rank, weak growth. It is monocarpic, spending its first year or two as a silver rosette before flowering once and dying.

directions: Grow in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun and withhold extra water once the rosette is established; Tower of Jewels spends its early life as a dense, silvery, bristled rosette before sending up a single narrow, tapering spike densely packed with thousands of small coral-red to salmon-pink flowers. The towering spike, often reaching 6-8 feet, is one of the most striking sights in dry-climate gardens and is intensely attractive to hummingbirds and bees during its weeks of bloom. After flowering the plant dies, so allow seed to scatter or collect and resow to maintain a planting over successive years. It performs best in Mediterranean and coastal California-type climates with dry summers and resents humid or wet conditions, which promote crown rot.

common_name: White Tower of Jewels (Giant White Echium)

planting.note: Sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; native only to a few cliffside sites on Tenerife, this species is more frost-tender than its red-flowered relative E. wildpretii and is best reserved for essentially frost-free, dry-summer coastal gardens or large containers that can be sheltered in winter.

directions: Plant in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun with shelter from hard frost; White Tower of Jewels forms a broad rosette of long, silvery, silky-haired leaves that, once mature, sends up a single dense, cylindrical spike thickly studded with small creamy-white flowers, reaching up to 10 feet in favorable sites. It is among the rarest and most dramatic of the Canary Island echiums in cultivation, valued for the striking contrast of its pale spike against the silver foliage, and draws steady bee activity during its bloom period. Keep it dry and lean, since overly rich soil or excess irrigation produces soft, floppy growth prone to collapse and rot. Being monocarpic, the rosette dies after flowering, so gardeners typically keep a succession of seedlings at different ages to maintain a continuous display.
